data.text/markdown:
Does buying/getting more compounds help your model?

The OpenADMET ExpansionRx challenge gives access to several ADME endpoints, and the results there showed that some endpoints benefit from adding external data into the training set. This notebook takes LogD as a case study, because public LogD data is available and easier to merge public/project data. The question it asks: if you have a budget, does buying 100 to 5,000 external compounds improve your project model, and at what stage does that stop being true? Past some point a local model may be good enough that external data adds nothing. It looks at three things together, the stage of the project (how much internal data you already have), the acquisition strategy (how you choose what to buy), and the model you train.

How to read it

Top to bottom: the data, then the precomputed effect, then a live round you run yourself. The precomputed sweeps compare an ensemble of tree-based models against Chemprop; the live section uses a small random-forest-style stack only, since running Chemprop in the browser would take hours rather than seconds. The chemical maps are precomputed too (locally you could regenerate them with umap installed).

Caveats worth carrying

  • One endpoint, a fixed number of datapoints, two model families and a handful of acquisition strategies. It is an example, not a survey.
  • A lot is precomputed, and the live section is deliberately kept to small data so the graphs move in seconds online. Local experiments could be run with more data and steps.
  • External compounds are sampled blind: LogD is revealed only after the compound is bought. A real campaign could sample far more cleverly, using information already available to ensure coverage of the project's chemistry.
  • In a real project you would do more on curation and model building, and you would not be limited to small datasets.
The repository behind this notebook has every script used to download, standardise and curate the data, and to run the sweeps that produced the assets loaded below.

data.text/markdown:
Repository

All the scripts are available at https://github.com/jeremycheminf/marimo-openadmet. It contains the scripts for data download, curation, model training and evaluation. A README and a pixi.toml let you rerun them to reproduce the data and results, or change the datasets, grid settings or models. The VS Code marimo extension was used to build this notebook and it was run with the pixi environment. It is designed for https://marimo.io/pages/events/notebook-competition-3; in production, more computational work would be performed to get better conclusions.

Dataset and curation steps

All the scripts for the data download and curation are in the repository. The OpenADMET dataset for the ExpansionRx challenge was downloaded and the LogD values extracted. For external data, the datasets from the RTLogD repository were used (https://github.com/myzhengSIMM/RTlogD/tree/main). SMILES were standardised with RDKit and all descriptors were also calculated with RDKit. LogD values were filtered to the -1 to 6 range to stay around the OpenADMET range. Processed data are available in the repository.

data.text/html:
Vendor/External file

A vendor offers 21,278 LogD measurements More data is usually better, but obtaining it can be costly. This notebook runs the purchase 392 times using different ways of mining the vendor set: random, similarity to the training set, uncertainty and diversity. In some active-learning settings a potency or a docking score gives a direction to optimise; LogD is a range with no such direction, so the usual directional algorithms (UCB with a Gaussian process, for example) do not apply here.
What the vendor charges -- the tiles above price the offer:

data.text/markdown:
1. Data available

Before any argument about buying: the label itself, in the data you own and in the data you would be buying. Note that in a project the test set distribution would be unknown, but a vendor may provide their distribution without individual data

2. Does buying help, and when?

For each run the test set is fixed and it is the OpenADMET test set. However the training varies. It consists of a fraction of the OpenADMET training set, sorted by compound ID to mimic a project progression, plus a number of compounds from the catalogue of LogD data. So fraction 10% + budget 500 = ~450 internal compounds plus 500 bought ones. The fraction moves up and 4 budgets are tested 100 / 500 / 1000 / 5000 (this is to keep some computation time reasonable and run on a laptop). The same purchases were simulated twice:
  • ensemble (RF + LightGBM + XGBoost over fixed ECFP+descriptors) -- 4 strategies (random + 3) x 10 fractions, 4 rounds each.
  • chemprop (a D-MPNN, 20 epochs) -- 4 strategies x 3 fractions, 10 rounds. Far more expensive, so only 3 fractions.
For ensemble, buying/adding data help at the start but then the model actually gets worse. When enough compounds are available, a 100% local model with this ML approach is better. But for chemprop, adding data is always helpful, even when 100% of the training set is used. The strategy of gaining data has an impact, but overall, the ML has more importance, in this particular case; a lot more work would be needed to generalise. Each panel is one starting position: how much internal data you already hold. Within a panel the model buys external compounds and is re-scored on the untouched test set. You can see model and strategy differences.

What the model actually predicts. Each point is one of the 2,155 test compounds: measured LogD against the prediction of the model trained at the stage and budget you pick below. Grey is the same stage with nothing bought. The Model dropdown and strategy selection above apply here too; random shows its first seed.

data.text/markdown: 3. What is the impact of how the selection is done?
4. Chemical space impact and similarity

data.text/html: Section 3 found that no acquisition strategy beats random. One potential reason here is that all the external compounds are not similar to the training and test sets. Against the ~21k external compounds it is 0.32 -- and 0% are above >0.7 high similarity threshold. Also, the test set contains 795 distinct Bemis-Murcko scaffolds. 112 of them appear in the training data. But only 2 appear anywhere in the external set. Compounds are not similar and the different acquisition ends up selecting from a diverse set. Similar compounds are still not that similar and using similarity as acquisition only takes from a small set; while diversity can be close to random in that particular case; or worse as it could select real outliers that are different from everything else.

data.text/markdown: 5. Model has a large impact

6. Live experiement

Everything above is precomputed. This part is running live when pressing the button. You can pick a strategy and it runs four real buy rounds against a 3,000-compound slice of the pool, scores on the same 2,155-compound test set, and compare your choice against random. The dataset is smaller than the offline one, so RMSE is worse but the direction over compound acquisition is similar. Also Random Forest is closer to the ensemble models than chemprop.

7. Data visualisation and chemical space map - UMAP

This is an example of visualisation where chemical map is drawn from external set, but you can enter SMILES and see where they will sit compared to the rest. You can see if the compounds are within dense area or outliers. The map is based on 2D fingerprint similarity.

data.text/html:
The goal was to see the impact of buying assay data to get better prediction.

What this experiments actually support

  1. Whether buying helps depends on the model you will train. For the tree ensemble it helps at the start but then quickly project data dominates; for chemprop the same purchases keep paying all the way Taking the ensemble alone: At 450 internal compounds, 5,000 bought compounds move test RMSE by about 0.12. By ~900 internal compounds that benefit is gone and it's in the noise.
  2. Strategies here didn't matter much. Across the strategy grid almost every cell sits inside random's own seed spread. Diversity, uncertainty and relevance-targeted. Only similarity shifted the chemistry to closer to training but it did worse on performance.
  3. The external set was never close to the target chemistry. Median nearest-neighbour Tanimoto from test to external is 0.32, and just 2 of 795 test scaffolds appear anywhere in the 21,278 compounds on offer.
  4. The biggest win had nothing to do with buying. Swapping the tree ensemble for a properly-trained chemprop improved RMSE by 0.204 on internal data alone -- larger than any purchase we simulated, at zero acquisition cost.

Some thoughts

  • Model first. Confirm the model you intend to train can use more data at all.
  • Then, check dataset coverage and acquisition, depending of the size random can do well.
  • However if the set to get data from is in order of millions, then more work approaches need to be tested.

Restrictions

  • Even if it's one of the largest data in the OpenADMET set, it's still small.
  • running Marimo locally could provide better live work, including chemprop, or tree family possible to run live; changing a cell at the top could then erun all analysis in one go which would be powerful (no need to precompute the data).
  • One endpoint, one split. It runs on LogD because LogD is the endpoint with a large public data with an assay that works with combining data together. The other assays in OpenADMET can benefit from external data, as the challenge showed, but their curation is more complex.
  • random was run with 5 seeds, others with less- Chemprop is limited. Single runs, no hyperparameter search and short training, because of the compute a full exploration would need.
  • The outcome may vary with other acquisition functions, models and hyperparameters.
